turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Before you go in, I've the observations done. Blood pressure is one thirty-eight over eighty-six, pulse is seventy-six, oxygen saturation ninety-eight percent, and the weight is seventy-two kilos.

[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Seventy-two, grand, though that cuff was fierce tight and I'm after a strong mug of tea, so I hope it isn't a false reading. I always feel the pressure jumps when I'm rushing for the bus.
[SEG0003] person_3 (DOCTOR): Come on in, the two of you. I'm Dr. Brennan. What has you here today?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): It's the stomach, Doctor, a burning pain, and the sleep has gone to pieces with it. I could write you a book on the ceiling at three in the morning.
[SEG0005] person_4 (CAREGIVER): The bad pain, I'd put it at three months. She was eating grand back in the autumn, Sunday dinners and all.

[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Three months? The burn sits under the breastbone and goes through to the back, worse after rashers or anything fried, and a sup of milk eases it a little. It's been on me since last winter, or the winter before, and I couldn't put a date on it. The Christmas pudding that year was a pure disaster.

[SEG0007] person_3 (DOCTOR): Let me say that back. The burn is under the breastbone after fried food, milk eases it, you place the start at last winter or the winter before and can't date it, and your carer has the bad patch at three months. I won't force a single date. Where exactly is it sitting now, and does it travel?

[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Top of the belly, and through to the back if I've been bold with the fry, which I already said, I know. Not a stab, more a hot coal, and then I'm burping for an hour, which is lovely in company. People pretend not to hear it and I pretend not to notice them pretending.
[SEG0009] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any vomiting with this?

[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): The dinners have been a saga, if you want the truth. Tuesday was stew and I left the onions out because onions repeat on me something shocking, Thursday was toast and tea, and the wine sits on it, and then I'm awake at two.
[SEG0011] person_3 (DOCTOR): We'll park the menu for a second. Have you actually vomited, or brought up any blood?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): No vomiting, and no blood, thank God. There's a sour taste in the mouth, like, but nothing comes up.
[SEG0013] person_3 (DOCTOR): And the bowels — any diarrhoea, constipation, or black stools?

[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): The bowels are grand, once a day, ordinary brown, nothing black. I watch the colour because my father had an ulcer, Lord have mercy, and they were forever asking him about it.
[SEG0015] person_3 (DOCTOR): Has the weight dropped at all?

[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): The clothes fit the same, so I don't think so, though I've not stood on the scales at home. The appetite is up and down — brown bread I'll take, a full dinner I often can't, and then I feel guilty for wasting good food.
[SEG0017] person_3 (DOCTOR): How many hours are you actually sleeping?

[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Four hours if I'm lucky, all broken, and it's the pain that wakes me. I say a decade of the rosary and then it's Lyric FM until the heating clicks on. Mad, isn't it, the things you do at that hour.
[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain, or shortness of breath, at night or otherwise?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No chest pain, and I'm not gasping or anything like that. I get myself into a fuss, sure, but the breathing is grand.
[SEG0021] person_3 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke, or take a drink?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): I never smoked, not even a puff behind the sheds. The drink is only socially, a glass if there's a do on.
[SEG0023] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Ah now, love, that's the polite version. Tell her about the evenings in the armchair.
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, actually, it's a bottle of wine most nights, perhaps. Red, nothing posh, just with the telly. I didn't want a lecture, but there it is.

[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): No lecture, I promise, and thank you for saying it straight. A bottle most nights can irritate the stomach and the liver, so the liver bloods are worth doing. What tablets are you on at the moment?

[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): There's the water tablet, the little white one, for the blood pressure. I think the dose is two and a half milligrams, or maybe five, I never read the box properly. And I use the pink Gaviscon from the chemist when the burn is up, and two paracetamol at night sometimes, more for the head than the belly.

[SEG0027] person_4 (CAREGIVER): She doesn't know the name and neither do I, it's just the water tablet from the surgery, years back. She misses it some mornings if she's rushing — I counted three still in the blister on Thursday.

[SEG0028] person_3 (DOCTOR): So the blood pressure is ongoing, and the water tablet for it has no name to hand, dose maybe two and a half or five milligrams, with some mornings missed. Gaviscon when it burns, and paracetamol some nights, I've got that. Any drug allergies at all?
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I'm not allergic to any tablet I know of.
[SEG0030] person_4 (CAREGIVER): There was penicillin, years ago. She came out in a rash and they stopped it, though she always says it might not have been that.

[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): I was sixteen or so, it was warm weather, and it could have been a heat rash, I honestly don't know. I've avoided penicillin since, just in case, which is probably daft if it wasn't even the cause.
[SEG0032] person_3 (DOCTOR): Were any tests done for the stomach or the liver before this?

[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): Bloods at the surgery, and I couldn't tell you when — last year, or the year before that. The nurse said the liver one was borderline, just a shade high, and they left it, no tablets or anything.
[SEG0034] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any surgery in the past?
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): None for me. My sister had the gallbladder out last spring and I nearly went with her for the company, but no, I've never been under the knife.
[SEG0036] person_4 (CAREGIVER): She bought those herbal sleep tablets too, the valerian ones, and they went in the drawer.
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, valerian, from the chemist, I took them for a few nights and stopped. They did nothing for the sleep and they smelled like old hay, if I'm honest.
[SEG0038] person_3 (DOCTOR): Hop up on the couch and I'll examine the tummy.
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): This couch is always freezing, I'll try not to jump. I tense when it's cold, so don't mind me if I do.
[SEG0040] person_3 (DOCTOR): Abdomen is soft, tender at the epigastrium, no guarding, and I can't feel any lump. The chest is clear and the heart sounds are fine.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Tender, yes, that's the spot, especially if you press just there. I thought you were going to find a lump the size of a turnip, the way it feels from the inside.

[SEG0042] person_3 (DOCTOR): This sounds like acid irritation of the stomach, a gastritis, likely stirred by the wine. I can't rule out a small ulcer, but there's nothing today that says you're bleeding.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): An ulcer is what took my father, so you'll understand I'm spinning a bit. If it's only the acid I can live with that, once I know which it is.

[SEG0044] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'll start you on omeprazole, twenty milligrams, by mouth, one capsule every morning half an hour before breakfast, and we'll do that for a month at least. Keep the Gaviscon for breakthrough if you need it.

[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): Before breakfast, half an hour, I can do that if I put the capsule by the kettle. The Gaviscon I'll leave on the bedside locker so I'm not rooting in the dark and waking the whole landing.

[SEG0046] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'm ordering a liver panel and a full blood count, and I'll see you back here in two weeks to go through them. If the pain hasn't settled by then, we might arrange a gastroscopy, a camera test, but only if we need it. If you vomit blood, or the stools turn black, or the pain gets severe, come straight in and don't wait for me.
[SEG0047] person_4 (CAREGIVER): And the wine — are you wanting it stopped dead?

[SEG0048] person_3 (DOCTOR): No command to stop dead. Bringing it down from a bottle most nights, even towards a glass, will help the stomach and the liver. I'd skip the fried food, and don't take ibuprofen or aspirin for that pain. Bring the water-tablet box to the next visit so we can name it and fix the dose.
[SEG0049] person_1 (NURSE): I'll take the liver panel and the full blood count next door now. It won't take long.
